sec.title: Objective
sec.p: This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of empagliflozin in acute myocardial infarction (AMI) treatment by synthesizing evidence from published randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane databases were thoroughly retrieved from inception to November 30, 2024, to identify eligible RCTs comparing empagliflozin with placebo in AMI treatment. The Cochrane Risk of Bias tool was leveraged to detect potential bias. The robustness of the results was examined via sensitivity analyses. Publication bias was evaluated via funnel plots and Egger’s test.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Data from 9 RCTs involving 7,237 AMI patients were analyzed. Meta-analysis revealed that empagliflozin significantly reduced the total hospitalization rate for heart failure (HF) in AMI patients in comparison to placebo (relative risk [RR] = 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.57–0.85). Additionally, empagliflozin significantly improved their ejection fraction (EF) (standard mean difference [SMD] = 1.01, 95% CI = 0.63–1.38), left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LVGLS) (SMD = −0.27, 95% CI = −0.48 to −0.06), body weight (SMD = −0.80, 95% CI = −1.15 to −0.45), and systolic blood pressure (SBP) (SMD = −0.54, 95% CI = −0.88 to −0.20). Statistically significant differences were not noted in other parameters (all p > 0.05). The incidence of adverse events (AEs), such as hepatic dysfunction, contrast-induced nephropathy, and urinary tract infections, did not differ significantly across groups (all p > 0.05). The GRADE rating indicated the evidence for HF hospitalization rate and body weight was of high certainty.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Empagliflozin lowers the total hospitalization rate for HF in AMI patients and significantly improves EF, LVGLS, body weight, and SBP without raising the likelihood of AEs.
Keywords: Empagliflozin, acute myocardial infarction, cardiovascular outcomes, randomized controlled trial, systematic review

list-item.p: This study aims to shed light on the efficacy and safety of empagliflozin in AMI treatment by synthesizing evidence from published randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
Empagliflozin reduces the total hospitalization rate for HF in AMI patients and significantly improves EF, LVGLS, body weight, and SBP without raising the likelihood of AEs.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is a predominant cause of global death and morbidity. It is characterized by complex pathophysiological mechanisms, including acute coronary artery occlusion, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and subsequent inflammation and oxidative stress [1]. There are advances in early reperfusion therapies, pharmacological interventions, and lifestyle modifications, which have significantly improved survival rates during the acute phase. Nevertheless, AMI patients remain at substantial long-term risk for adverse outcomes such as heart failure (HF), left ventricular dysfunction (LVD), and cardiovascular mortality (CVM) [1]. Current therapeutic strategies are partially effective but demonstrate notable limitations in long-term myocardial protection and cardiac function improvement.

Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor initially developed for treating type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), has recently garnered attention for its role in the management of cardiovascular diseases [2]. Multiple studies have revealed the broad cardiovascular protective effects of empagliflozin like reducing cardiac preload, ameliorating myocardial energy metabolism, attenuating inflammation and oxidative stress, and improving vascular function [3]. Specifically, in patients with chronic HF and those at high cardiovascular risk, empagliflozin has been proven to significantly reduce the rates of HF hospitalization and CVM [4]. These findings lay a theoretical groundwork for investigating the myocardial protective effects of empagliflozin following AMI.

However, while the efficacy of empagliflozin in HF and chronic cardiovascular conditions is well-established, its role in AMI patients is elusive [5]. Existing studies have yielded inconsistent results: some suggest a potential reduction in HF hospitalization rates, but no consensus has been reached regarding its effects on all-cause mortality (ACM) or CVM [6]. A recently published EMPACT-MI trial [7] reported that empagliflozin did not notably lower the likelihood of first hospitalization for HF or ACM in post-AMI HF individuals in contrast to placebo, though it did decrease the total number of HF hospitalizations. Additionally, the specific efficacy of empagliflozin across different left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) subgroups and its long-term impact on ventricular remodeling remain to be elucidated [8].

This study aims to clarify the efficacy and safety of empagliflozin in AMI patients through a systematic review and meta-analysis of available clinical evidence. The findings will lay scientific groundwork for formulating better clinical research and therapeutic strategies. Figure 1 illustrates the workflow of this study.

sec.title: Protocol registration
sec.p: The current meta-analysis has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) with Registration No.: CRD42024620001. There were no deviations from the original protocol. This study adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [9].

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: The inclusion criteria were as follows:

list-item.p: Population (P): Patients diagnosed with AMI, including those with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) or non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI);

Outcomes (O): Clinical outcomes related to AMI, including ACM, total HF hospitalization rates, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), white blood cell (WBC) count, interleukin-6 (IL-6), ketone bodies, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR); N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), body weight, left ventricular filling pressure (E/e’) ratio, left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LVGLS), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), EF, systolic blood pressure(SBP), diastolic blood pressure(DBP), liver function impairment, contrast-induced nephropathy, and urinary tract infections;

sec.p: The exclusion criteria were as follows:

list-item.p: Case reports, reviews, letters, conference abstracts, and commentaries;
Studies with overlapping or duplicate data;
When data was missing, the original data was extracted after contacting the corresponding author. Data that could be obtained from the corresponding author are excluded.

sec.title: Literature search
sec.p: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, were searched from database inception to November 30, 2024. The search was performed using predefined keywords: ‘empagliflozin’ and ‘myocardial infarction’. The PubMed was retrieved with words as follows: (((‘empagliflozin’ [Supplementary Concept]) OR ((((BI 10773) OR (BI-10773)) OR (BI10773)) OR (Jardiance))) AND ((‘Myocardial Infarction’ [Mesh]) OR ((((((((Myocardial Infarctions) OR (Heart Attack)) OR (Heart Attacks)) OR (Myocardial Infarct)) OR (Myocardial Infarcts)) OR (Cardiovascular Stroke)) OR (Cardiovascular Strokes)) OR (AMI)))) AND (random*). The search strategies for other databases are detailed in Supplementary Table 1. Additionally, manual screening of references from relevant systematic reviews was undertaken to ensure the inclusion of all pertinent studies.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Two researchers (LP and JF) independently assessed eligible studies and extracted data from them. Any dissents were addressed via discussions involving all co-authors until a consensus was reached. Extracted data were the first author, publication year, country, study population and length, intervention, sample size, age, sex, BMI, follow-up duration, as well as outcome measures.

The primary outcomes were ACM and total hospitalization rates for HF in patients with AMI. Secondary outcomes included levels of hsCRP, WBC, IL-6, ketone bodies, HbA1c, eGFR, NT-proBNP, body weight, E/e’ ratio, LVGLS, TAPSE, EF, SBP and DBP, liver function impairment, contrast-induced nephropathy, and urinary tract infections.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The quality of the encompassed RCTs was examined via the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool [10]. This tool assesses seven domains: (I) random sequence generation, (II) allocation concealment, (III) blinding of participants and personnel, (IV) blinding of outcome assessment, (V) incomplete outcome data, (VI) selective reporting, as well as (VII) other sources of bias. Each domain was rated as low risk, unclear risk, or high risk of bias.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Pooled effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated through a random-effects model for assessing the efficacy and safety of empagliflozin in AMI individuals. Categorical ­variables were analyzed through risk ratios (RR) and 95% CI, while continuous variables were ­analyzed via standardized mean difference (SMD) and 95% CI. Heterogeneity across studies was detected through Cochran’s Q test and Higgins’ I2 statistic. Significant heterogeneity was defined as I2 > 50% or p < 0.1. Sensitivity analyses were undertaken to test the robustness of the outcomes. Publication bias was detected via funnel plots and Egger’s test, with p < 0.05 denoting statistical significance. Every statistical analysis was executed with the help of STATA 15.0 and Review Manager 5.4. Additionally, the GRADE approach was employed to classify the quality of the evidence for each outcome as very low, low, moderate, or high certainty [11].

sec.title: Literature screening and characteristics of included studies
sec.p: An initial search across four major databases yielded 840 articles. After 293 duplicate articles, 4 non-English studies, and 18 animal experiments were ostracized. The titles and abstracts of the rest were checked, and 443 articles were subsequently ostracized. Subsequently, the full texts of 82 studies were checked. 73 were excluded for these reasons: irrelevance to AMI (n = 41), lack of relevance to empagliflozin (n = 18), and absence of outcome indicators (n = 14). Ultimately, 9 RCTs [7,12–19] were selected in our meta-analysis (Figure 2). The foregoing studies published from 2020 to 2024 involved patient populations ranging from 42 to 6,522 individuals. The cumulative sample size was 7,237 patients. Among the included studies, one study [7] was conducted across multiple countries and centers. Four studies were conducted in Austria, including one original RCT [19] and three secondary data analyses based on the original RCT [12,13,17]. Two studies were conducted in Japan, comprising one original RCT [18] and one secondary data analysis based on the original RCT [16]. One study was conducted in Iran [14] and Sweden [15]. Of the included studies, four [7,14,18,19] reported binary outcome data for empagliflozin compared with placebo in relation to AMI endpoints. Eight studies [12–19] reported continuous outcome data for empagliflozin compared with placebo. Additionally, eight studies [7,12–14,16–19] used a 10 mg dose of empagliflozin in the experimental group, whereas one study [15] used a 25 mg dose. The baseline characteristics of eligible studies are detailed in Table 1.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The risk of bias assessment is illustrated in Figure 3. All 9 included RCTs employed random sequence generation. Eight studies [12–19] were well-designed with no significant flaws, and all items were rated as ‘low risk’. However, one study [7] had a loss-to-follow-up rate exceeding 20% and was assessed as ‘high risk’.

caption.p: (A) Summary of the risk of bias for the included studies; (B) Risk of bias for each individual study.

sec.title: ACM
sec.p: Three studies [7,14,19] reported the results of a categorical meta-analysis on ACM in patients with AMI. The findings demonstrated that, in contrast to the placebo group, the empagliflozin group did not exhibit a decline in ACM (RR = 1.0, 95% CI = 0.52–1.90, p > 0.99). No significant heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 8%, p = 0.34) (Figure 4A).

caption.p: (A) Forest Plot comparing the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding ACM (categorical variable); (B) Forest plot comparing the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding the total hospitalization rate for HF (categorical variable). Notes: CI, confidence interval.

sec.title: Total hospitalization rate for H
sec.p: Four studies [7,14,18,19] reported the categorical data for the total hospitalization rate for HF in AMI patients. In comparison to the placebo group, empagliflozin significantly lowered the total HF hospitalization rate (RR = 0.70, 95% CI = 0.57–0.85, p = 0.0004). Significant heterogeneity was not present (I2 = 0%, p = 0.67) (Figure 4B).

sec.title: Secondary outcomes
sec.p: Our study demonstrated that empagliflozin had significant effects on the following outcomes in AMI patients: weight reduction (SMD = −0.80, 95% CI = −1.15 to −0.45, p < 0.00001), LVGLS (SMD = −0.27, 95% CI = −0.48 to −0.06, p = 0.01), EF (SMD = 1.01, 95% CI = 0.63–1.38, p < 0.00001), and SBP (SMD = −0.54, 95% CI = −0.88 to −0.20, p = 0.002). Detailed results are displayed in Supplementary Figure 1.

Significant effects of empagliflozin were not noted for the following outcomes: hs-CRP (SMD = −0.29, 95% CI = −0.85 to 0.26, p = 0.30), WBC count (SMD = −0.46, 95% CI = −1.58 to 0.66, p = 0.42), IL-6 (SMD = 0.43, 95% CI = −0.12 to 0.97, p = 0.12), ketone bodies (SMD = 2.95, 95% CI = −1.82 to 7.72, p = 0.23), HbA1c (SMD = −0.05, 95% CI = −0.38 to 0.29, p = 0.79), eGFR (SMD = 0.18, 95% CI = −0.16 to 0.51, p = 0.30), NT-proBNP (SMD = −0.19, 95% CI = −0.59 to 0.21, p = 0.35), E/e’ ratio (SMD = −0.55, 95% CI = −1.54 to 0.44, p = 0.28), TAPSE (SMD = 0.09, 95% CI = −0.12 to 0.30, p = 0.38), and DBP (SMD = −0.27, 95% CI = −0.60 to 0.07, p = 0.12). Detailed results are presented in Supplementary Figure 1.

sec.title: Adverse drug reactions
sec.p: Our meta-analysis did not reveal significant differences between the empagliflozin and placebo groups in the incidence of liver dysfunction (RR = 2.01, 95% CI = 0.55–7.41, p = 0.29) based on three studies [7,18,19]. Heterogeneity was minimal (I2 = 5%, p = 0.35) (Figure 5A). Similarly, two studies [7,14] showed no significant differences in contrast-induced nephropathy (RR = 0.93, 95% CI = 0.43–2.02, p = 0.85; I2 = 0%, p = 0.87) (Figure 5B). In addition, two studies [14,19] found no statistically significant differences in urinary tract infections (RR = 1.76, 95% CI = 0.72–4.26, p = 0.21; I2 = 0%, p = 0.47) (Figure 5C).

caption.p: (A) Forest Plot comparing the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding liver function impairment (categorical variable); (B) Forest plot comparing the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding contrast-induced renal impairment (categorical variable); (C) Forest plot comparing the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding urinary tract infections (categorical variable). Notes: CI, confidence interval.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: Sensitivity analysis indicated that the efficacy of empagliflozin on ACM (Figure 6A), liver dysfunction (Figure 6B), and hs-CRP (Figure 6C) in AMI individuals was not significantly impacted by any single study. However, the results for HF total hospitalization rate (Figure 6D) were affected by one included study. After Butler et al.’s study (2024) was removed, the pooled result was (OR = 0.47, 95% CI = 0.20–1.08, p = 0.07), with no significant change in heterogeneity (I2 = 0%, p = 0.74). Sensitivity analysis was not performed for other outcomes reported in limited studies (n = 2).

caption.p: (A) Sensitivity analysis of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding ACM; (B) Sensitivity analysis of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding liver function impairment; (C) Sensitivity analysis of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding hsCRP; (D) Sensitivity analysis of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding total hospitalization rate for HF.

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: Egger’s test and funnel plots were leveraged to detect publication bias. Funnel plots for ACM (Figure 7A), HF total hospitalization rate (Figure 7B), liver dysfunction (Figure 7C), and hsCRP (Figure 7D) appeared symmetric. The Egger’s test results reflected no significant publication bias for ACM (p = 0.786), HF total hospitalization rate (p = 0.336), liver dysfunction (p = 0.099), and hsCRP (p = 0.057).

caption.p: (A) Funnel plot of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding ACM; (B) Funnel plot of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding the total hospitalization rate for HF; (C) Funnel plot of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding liver function impairment; (D) Funnel plot of the relationship between empagliflozin and placebo regarding hsCRP. Notes: RR, relative risk; SMD, standard mean difference.

sec.title: GRADE rating
sec.p: The GRADE rating for all categorical and continuous variables in AMI patients classified the evidence as follows: low-certainty evidence for ketone bodies, hs-CRP, leukocyte count, IL-6, and E/e’ ratio; moderate-certainty evidence for ACM, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, eGFR, LVGLS, TAPSE, EF, SBP and DBP, liver dysfunction, contrast-induced nephropathy, and urinary tract infections; and high-certainty evidence for HF total hospitalization rate and weight. Detailed GRADE ratings are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, was originally developed for T2DM treatment. However, in recent years, its potential in the management of cardiovascular diseases has garnered widespread attention [20]. Previous studies have unequivocally demonstrated that empagliflozin provides significant protective benefits. For example, It is effective in reducing hospitalization rates for HF, CVM, chronic kidney disease [21], and high-risk cardiovascular diseases [22]. Given that patients with AMI face a heightened risk of HF and mortality [23], tailored therapeutic strategies for this population warrant special consideration. In this context, investigating the application of empagliflozin in AMI patients is of critical significance. It may be beneficial for alleviating congestion, improving cardiac function, and reducing myocardial remodeling [24]. However, in comparison to its well-established role in chronic cardiovascular conditions, evidence supporting empagliflozin in the management of AMI remains limited. Therefore, consolidating existing research findings to clarify the cardioprotective role and mechanisms of empagliflozin in post-AMI management is particularly important.

In this meta-analysis, data from nine RCTs, encompassing 7,237 patients, were systematically reviewed. Our findings reveal that, compared with placebo, empagliflozin significantly reduced the overall hospitalization rate for HF in AMI patients. Furthermore, empagliflozin was more effective than placebo in improving clinical parameters, such as body weight, EF, LVGLS, and SBP. However, statistically significant differences were not detected across groups with regard to ACM, hs-CRP, WBC count, IL-6, ketone bodies, HbA1C, eGFR, NT-proBNP, E/e’ ratio, TAPSE, or DBP. Similarly, there were no significant differences in safety outcomes, including liver function impairment, contrast-induced nephropathy, or urinary tract infections. Sensitivity analyses revealed instability in the results of hospitalization rates, whereas the results of parameters such as hs-CRP, ACM, and liver function impairment remained unaffected by any single study. Egger’s test indicated no publication bias for outcomes including ACM, HF hospitalization rates, liver function impairment, and hsCRP.

Recent studies have explored the influence of empagliflozin on left heart parameters in acute coronary syndrome (ACS), with a relevant article recently published. This article included only four studies published between 2019 and 2022, encompassing 701 ACS patients. The findings demonstrated significant improvements in echocardiographic parameters, including left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVi), left ventricular mass index (LVMi), and E/e’ ratio, in the empagliflozin-treated group in contrast to the control group [25]. In a meta-analysis by Sinha et al. incorporating nine studies, ACS patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors exhibited a significantly lower likelihood of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), ACM, cardiovascular death, and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations than the control group [26]. However, previous studies have primarily focused on ACS populations without specifically analyzing empagliflozin as the experimental group. Moreover, none of the aforementioned articles employed sensitivity analysis or Egger’s test to assess the robustness and publication bias of their results. Our study included the most recent and largest RCT published in 2024 [7] and found that empagliflozin did not reduce ACM in patients. Additionally, our meta-analysis encompassed a wide range of clinical outcomes, including ACM, total hospitalizations for HF, laboratory parameters, cardiac indices, and adverse drug reactions. Sensitivity analysis, publication bias assessment, and GRADE methodology were employed to ensure the reliability of our findings. This is the first and most comprehensive meta-analysis summarizing the correlation of empagliflozin with clinical outcomes in AMI individuals.

Interestingly, through sensitivity analysis, the dichotomous results for total HF hospitalization rates were influenced by the study by Butler et al. (2024). Upon excluding this study, reanalyzed data showed no statistically significant variance in total HF hospitalization rates across the two groups (OR = 0.47, 95% CI = 0.20–1.08, p = 0.07). The reason lies in the disproportionately high weight of the Butler 2024 study in the pooled analysis, whose large sample size (6,522 patients) [7], significantly exceeds that of the other three included studies. This disproportionate weight likely contributed to the instability of the sensitivity analysis. Butler’s large-scale RCT on AMI in 2024 showed that in comparison to placebo, empagliflozin did not reduce the composite risk of first hospitalization for HF and ACM. However, in its exploratory endpoint analysis, the total number of HF-related hospitalizations was significantly lower in the empagliflozin group compared to the placebo group. Moreover, prior trials focusing on patients with HF or those with T2DM and atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases have consistently shown that SGLT2 inhibitor treatment significantly reduces the relative risk (RR) of HF hospitalization compared to placebo [27–29]. Moreover, a secondary analysis based on the EMPACT-MI trial revealed that empagliflozin decreased the time to first HF hospitalization and the total number of HF hospitalizations in both STEMI and non-STEMI patients, irrespective of the presence of type 2 diabetes [30]. Therefore, it is posited that retaining the Butler 2024 study in the analysis enhances the authenticity and reliability of the findings. Empagliflozin may effectively reduce the total hospitalization rate for HF in AMI patients.

The GRADE classification indicates that the continuous variables of ketone bodies, hs-CRP, leukocytes, IL-6, and E/e’ ratio are of low evidence quality and exhibit significant heterogeneity (I2 > 50% across all). This heterogeneity may arise from the limited sample size of the included studies (mean N = 2), variations in empagliflozin treatment duration and dosage, and inconsistent laboratory measurement units. For instance, in Lundin’s RCT [15], 44 patients were enrolled, with empagliflozin 25 mg serving as the control group. Conversely, Mozawa’s study [16] included 96 participants. These factors likely contributed to the high heterogeneity and low evidence level. Hence, future research should prioritize increasing sample sizes and minimizing heterogeneity to enhance the robustness and reliability of conclusions.

Our findings unraveled that empagliflozin demonstrated significant advantages in reducing HF-related hospitalization rates, improving cardiac parameters (e.g. EF and LVGLS), and lowering body weight and SBP among AMI patients. The underlying physiological mechanisms may involve multiple pathways, including anti-inflammatory, metabolic, and antioxidative effects. It is well-established that post-AMI inflammatory responses and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels are key contributors to cardiomyocyte apoptosis and ventricular remodeling [31]. Inflammatory markers like hs-CRP and IL-6 have been proven to mitigate NF-κB signaling activation and reduce the release of pro-inflammatory mediators, as evidenced by plenty of studies [32]. Empagliflozin’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidative properties play a crucial role in improving myocardial function [20,33]. Its involvement in these mechanisms likely correlates with the observed reduction in HF-related hospitalizations, suggesting that empagliflozin may alleviate myocardial inflammatory burden and decrease the incidence of adverse cardiovascular events after AMI. It is noteworthy that Benedikt et al. found that, in contrast to the placebo group, the empagliflozin group exhibited a reduction in inflammatory biomarkers (including IL-6, hs-CRP, neutrophils, NLR, and PLR) within the first 26 weeks. However, no significant difference was observed between the two groups after 26 weeks [13]. Similarly, after pooling the data from the eligible studies, no significant impact of empagliflozin on inflammation-related markers, such as IL-6, hs-CRP, and neutrophils, was found in the overall analysis. This may arise from the considerable heterogeneity in study parameters, and lack of relevant analyses concerning the temporal relationship between empagliflozin and inflammatory markers in the studies. It is also suggested that future research should focus on this aspect. Additionally, empagliflozin’s ability to elevate ketone body levels may provide an efficient energy source for ischemic myocardium [12,34]. This metabolic shift could be a key mechanism underlying the improvements in EF and LVGLS. Ketone bodies exhibit higher oxidative efficiency and produce fewer ROS. This further mitigates myocardial damage caused by oxidative stress after AMI, preserves cardiomyocyte function and prevents further ventricular remodeling [35].

Moreover, the protective effects of empagliflozin on mitochondrial function are pivotal in myocardial protection [36]. Ischemia-reperfusion injury from AMI disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential, increases ROS production, and accelerates cardiomyocyte death [37]. Empagliflozin stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential, helping to maintain mitochondrial dynamic balance and promoting cardiomyocyte survival [38]. These mechanisms likely contributed to the observed reductions in HF hospitalization rates and improvements in EF, as demonstrated in this study. In summary, empagliflozin exerts multifaceted effects on AMI. These effects include metabolic shifts, anti-inflammatory and antioxidative actions, and mitochondrial protection. The foregoing provides a theoretical basis for its clinical benefits in reducing HF-related hospitalizations and enhancing cardiac function recovery. Future studies should further explore the relationship between these mechanisms and clinical outcomes to elucidate the specific roles of empagliflozin in diverse AMI patient populations.

Our meta-analysis has limitations that warrant consideration. Firstly, the studies encompassed in this study exhibit notable differences, such as varying intervention drug regimens, different drug dosages, whether combined with other treatments, and inconsistent follow-up durations, which possibly lead to varying degrees of heterogeneity. Moreover, the patients in these studies come from different countries and regions. Given that this is a re-analysis of data from multiple single-center studies, the foregoing factors may introduce unavoidable selection bias and confounding effects in the research. Second, heterogeneity ranging from low to high was observed among the included studies. Variability in AMI subtypes, small sample sizes in certain subgroup analyses, and differences in follow-up intervals may contribute to the observed heterogeneity. However, due to the limited number of outcome measures, subgroup analyses could not be performed. Therefore, a cautious interpretation of the findings is necessitated. These key issues must be solved in future research to avoid overestimating the efficacy and safety of treatment. Prospective, high-quality, and multicenter clinical trials are needed to verify the foregoing results. The strengths of our study lie in its basis on the largest and most up-to-date RCT data currently available. This study systematically assesses the significant benefits and safety profile of empagliflozin in AMI treatment, providing unprecedented high-quality evidence in this field. Compared to previous studies, our research encompasses a broader range of clinical and laboratory outcomes and employs rigorous sensitivity analyses and bias assessment methods. Therefore, the reliability and scientific validity of the results are ensured. These findings offer the latest evidence-based support for the clinical use of empagliflozin in the treatment of AMI patients.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis demonstrates the significant effects of empagliflozin in reducing the total HF-related hospitalization rate and ameliorating EF, LVGLS, body weight, and SBP in AMI patients. While our study is limited by small sample sizes, high heterogeneity, and potential selection bias, it consolidates the largest and most recent RCT data, further confirming the efficacy and safety of empagliflozin in AMI treatment. These findings provide the latest evidence-based insights into the precise clinical management of AMI. Nevertheless, future studies involving larger sample sizes and multicenter RCTs are necessary to validate these findings.
